 Scoring them 
 The verdict 
 TL;DR 
 Related 
 The household NAS is usually backed up well. The Windows laptops and desktops that create most of the family’s actual files usually aren’t. The reason is rarely the NAS: it’s the agent on each Windows machine, which has to cope with open files, laptops that are asleep at 2 a.m., users who never look at a backup status, and the day a machine dies and someone needs it back exactly as it was.
 This guide compares the five agents people actually use for this, against a Linux NAS (a Debian box, TrueNAS, or anything with Samba and a ZFS pool):
 UrBackup : client–server, file and image backups, built for this exact job.
 Veeam Agent for Microsoft Windows, Free edition : image backups with polished recovery media.
 Kopia : a file-level backup tool with deduplication and a GUI.
 restic : a file-level backup tool, scripted, with deduplication.
 Duplicati : a file-level backup tool with a web interface, aimed at non-technical users.
 I tested UrBackup, Kopia and restic on a Windows 11 Pro 25H2 machine backing up to a Debian 13 NAS on the same LAN, including a full bare-metal restore. Veeam and Duplicati weren’t tested here; what I say about them comes from their documentation and is marked as such.
 The real split: image or files
 Every other difference matters less than this one.
 Image-based agents (UrBackup’s image mode, Veeam) copy the disk’s used blocks: Windows, programs, settings and files together. A restore puts the whole machine back. If a laptop’s drive dies, you boot a recovery stick, restore, and the user’s desktop comes back as they left it, with their programs, printers and browser profiles.
 File-based agents (Kopia, restic, Duplicati, UrBackup’s file mode) copy chosen folders. A restore gives you files. If the drive dies, you install Windows from scratch, reinstall the programs, and then restore the files on top.
 For a single deleted document, both work. For a dead drive, the image saves an afternoon or more of reinstalling, per machine. For ransomware, both work if the backups can’t be reached from the infected PC (more on that below).
 Most households need both: an image now and then, so a dead drive is a quick fix, and frequent file backups of the folders people actually change. UrBackup is the only one of the five that does both from one agent and one server.
 The test setup
 Windows side : Windows 11 Pro 25H2 (build 26200), 4 vCPU, 6 GB, 64 GB disk with 24.8 GB used, a local user with a normal profile. It ran on a Proxmox host as a VM, which matters later for the bare-metal test.
 NAS side : Debian 13 in a container with a ZFS-backed disk, running UrBackup Server 2.5.38 and Samba 4.22 with a share for the file-level tools.
 Network : same gigabit LAN, different physical hosts.
 Versions : UrBackup Client 2.5.32, restic 0.19.1, Kopia 0.23.1.
 The backup source for the file-level comparison was the user’s profile folder, C:\Users\demo : about 1.5 GB in 6,300 files, including the usual open-while-logged-in files (the registry hive NTUSER.DAT , Edge’s profile databases and caches, Windows’ communication databases).
 Volume Shadow Copy: the correctness test
 Windows locks files that are open. A backup tool that just opens files one by one fails on those, and the failures are easy to miss: the backup “completes” with warnings nobody reads. Volume Shadow Copy (VSS) fixes this: the tool asks Windows for a frozen, point-in-time view of the volume and reads from that instead, so locked files are read, and the files in the backup are consistent with each other.
 All five agents can use VSS. The question is whether it’s on by default and whether it actually engages. I ran restic and Kopia with VSS off and on, against the same profile folder, and counted the errors by type:

 What this means in practice:
 Without VSS, 72 files were silently missing from the restic backup , including NTUSER.DAT (the user’s registry: their settings for every program) and its transaction logs, Edge’s databases and Windows’ mail and calendar store. The backup reported success with errors.
 With VSS, every locked file was read. The snapshot showed 6,319 files with VSS against 6,250 without.
 restic’s 48 remaining errors are harmless : they’re the “app execution alias” stubs in AppData\Local\Microsoft\WindowsApps (small reparse points that let you type winget or wt ). restic reports them as an “irregular” file type it doesn’t store. Kopia skips them silently.
 Kopia’s default is never : you have to set the policy. It’s kopia policy set <path> --enable-volume-shadow-copy=when-available (or always , to fail if a snapshot can’t be made).
 restic needs the flag on every run : restic backup --use-fs-snapshot . Without it, it doesn’t use VSS.
 Both need administrator rights for VSS. restic’s documentation notes the error you get otherwise ( E_ACCESSDENIED ), and Kopia simply can’t create the snapshot. In a scheduled task, that means Run with highest privileges , or running as SYSTEM.
 UrBackup used VSS without being asked: its log shows the shadow copy being made for C:\ at the start of the file backup. Veeam is image-based and snapshots by design. Duplicati can use VSS through its snapshot policy, but only when it runs with enough privileges (as the Windows service rather than the tray app); our Duplicati in 2026 guide covers that trap.
 The restore drill
 A backup isn’t proven until something comes back out of it. From the VSS runs of both tools, I restored the user’s NTUSER.DAT , the file most likely to be missing:
 restic restored it at 1,835,008 bytes , the same size as the live file, in under a second.
 Kopia’s full restore of the 1.5 GB profile took 136 seconds to a local folder, and NTUSER.DAT came back at the same 1,835,008 bytes.
 One trap on the way: NTUSER.DAT is a hidden file, so a plain Get-ChildItem (or Explorer with default settings) doesn’t show it in the restore folder. I first thought the restore had failed. Use Get-ChildItem -Force or show hidden files.
 Two traps when the backup runs as SYSTEM
 Backups should run unattended, which usually means as the SYSTEM account or as a service. Both file-level tools hit a snag there in my testing.
 Mapped drives and SMB credentials. Trying to map the NAS share from a SYSTEM session failed with Windows error 1312 (“A specified logon session does not exist”). Drive letters and saved credentials belong to a user’s logon session, and a service session doesn’t have the same one. I ran the restic and Kopia tests as a scheduled task under the user’s account, with Run with highest privileges so VSS worked, and the share connected fine there.
 For a deployment you leave alone, avoid SMB credentials altogether and give the agents a repository they reach over HTTP or SFTP instead:
 restic has rest-server , which also supports an append-only mode, so a compromised PC can’t delete its own backups.
 Kopia can run as a repository server on the NAS, and clients connect to it with per-user credentials.
 UrBackup and Veeam don’t have this problem: UrBackup talks its own protocol to its server, and Veeam stores credentials for its target in the job.
 Kopia and the Windows credential store. Creating the Kopia repository from that session failed with “error saving password in OS keyring”, for the same logon-session reason. The fix is --no-persist-credentials and supplying the password another way (the KOPIA_PASSWORD environment variable, or a password file only the backup account can read). On a normal desktop, running KopiaUI as the user, the keyring works.
 UrBackup: what the test showed
 UrBackup is a server on the NAS plus a small client service on each PC. The server decides when backups happen, based on when each client is online, which is exactly what laptops need.
 Setup, and a first-run trap
 Installing the server on Debian was the .deb from UrBackup’s download site and one question: where to store backups. Two things then went wrong, both worth knowing:
 The backup folder must belong to the urbackup user. I created /srv/backup/urbackup as root, and the server logged “No permission to access” until I ran chown -R urbackup:urbackup on it.
 The silent client had nothing to back up. I installed the “NoTray” client silently ( /S ), which has no tray icon for choosing folders. The server found it within a minute through LAN broadcast, immediately started a full file backup, and failed it with “no backup dirs”, then backed off for 40 minutes. The fix is server-side: set Default directories to backup in the server’s file backup settings (I used C:\Users ). For a family fleet, setting this on the server is the better design anyway: nobody at the PCs has to choose anything.
 File and image backups
 Once it had folders to back up, UrBackup ran a full file backup and then, on its own schedule, a full image backup. It found the client and scheduled both without being asked. The numbers:
 Backup 
 Data 
 Transferred 
 Time 
 Average speed 
 Full file backup of C:\Users 
 2.51 GB 
 1.90 GB (compressed) 
 4 min 40 s 
 84 Mbit/s 
 Full image of C: 
 17.7 GB of used blocks 
 15.6 GB (compressed) 
 7 min 21 s 
 313 Mbit/s 
 A few details from the logs:
 It followed the All Users link into C:\ProgramData , so a backup of C:\Users also includes ProgramData. That’s usually what you want (it holds program settings), but it’s bigger than you might expect.
 The image backup also took the EFI system partition and the recovery partition , not just C:. That’s what makes a bare-metal restore bootable.
 Images only cover used blocks , so a 64 GB disk with 25 GB used became a 15.6 GB image.
 An interrupted backup leaves its partial files behind. I restarted the server during the first image attempt, and its 2.3 GB of partial data stayed in the client’s folder, marked incomplete. Check that the server’s cleanup removes them, rather than deleting files under its backup folder by hand.
 The file-backup speed is lower than the image speed because file backups do per-file work: hashing, checking for duplicates across clients, and writing many small files.
 The bare-metal restore
 This is the part most comparisons skip, and the reason to choose an image-based tool. I created an empty VM on a different Proxmox host (the image came from a host with an Intel Core i7-10700, and the new one has a Core i5-7500T; both VMs pass the host CPU through, so Windows saw a different CPU). It had a fresh UEFI disk, a fresh TPM, a different display adapter and an empty 64 GB disk.
 Then:
 Booted UrBackup’s restore ISO (version 2.4.2, built in 2022). It booted under UEFI with Secure Boot keys enrolled.
 Chose the text interface and a keyboard layout. 
 It searched the LAN, found the server and listed the backed-up computer by name. It then listed the image backups by date and volume.
 Picked the target disk and confirmed the overwrite.
 The restore ran for about five minutes and reported success. It then offered: restart, “Make Windows bootable on different hardware”, restore another volume, or stop.
 Restarted with the ISO removed. Windows 11 booted straight to the user’s desktop.
 So a dead disk on this machine is a five-minute restore plus a reboot, with nothing to reinstall. I didn’t need the “different hardware” option because the disk controller type was the same (SATA) on both VMs; that option is for when it isn’t, for example restoring onto a machine with an NVMe or RAID controller Windows has never seen. A different CPU, TPM and display adapter didn’t stop it booting.
 Advertisement 
 Two cautions:
 The restore CD found the server without asking for credentials , because my test server had no admin account set. Set one up on a real server: anyone who can boot a stick on your LAN could otherwise pull any machine’s image.
 A VM-to-VM test is the friendly case. Real hardware brings real driver differences: a restore from an old desktop onto a new laptop may need the “different hardware” option, or may not boot at all. UrBackup’s own manual warns that some hardware changes can make Windows bluescreen after a restore. Test a restore onto the hardware you’d actually use, before you need it.
 Laptops
 UrBackup’s design suits laptops: the server notices a client when it appears on the network (it broadcasts for clients about every 50 seconds, per its manual) and starts any backup that’s due. Nothing depends on the laptop being awake at a fixed time. Its manual also describes an internet mode , off by default, where clients back up to the server over the internet when they’re away from home, and alerts by email when a machine hasn’t been backed up for a set time. Our guide to backing up family laptops over Tailscale covers the remote case in more depth.
 Veeam Agent Free: image backups with the best recovery media
 I didn’t test Veeam here; this section is from Veeam’s documentation.
 Veeam Agent for Microsoft Windows has a Free edition that needs no licence. Its help centre lists what the Free edition leaves out: one backup job only , no backup windows or custom retry settings, no synthetic full backups, and no direct backup to object storage. The one job can target a local drive, a network shared folder, or a Veeam backup repository. Veeam’s forum staff have said the Free edition may be used in your own company but not to provide services to third parties. Downloading it from Veeam’s site means filling in a form and verifying an email address.
 What Veeam does well:
 Recovery media : you create a bootable USB stick or ISO from the agent itself. It’s built on Windows’ own recovery environment (WinRE), so it starts with Windows’ drivers, and Veeam’s user guide has a section on adding drivers to it for hardware it doesn’t recognise. That’s the main reason people recommend Veeam for “restore onto different hardware”.
 Backup to a shared folder : the NAS share works as a target. Store the credentials in the job.
 Its limits for a family fleet:
 Each PC is managed on its own. There’s no central server in the Free edition: you set up each machine, and nothing tells you centrally that one stopped backing up.
 One job per PC. That’s one image job, or one file-level job, not both.
 It isn’t open source , and the Free edition’s terms can change.
 That’s why it’s the right tool for the one machine that must restore onto different hardware , and less suited to a fleet you administer.
 Kopia and restic: file-level, deduplicated, scriptable
 Kopia and restic are close relatives: both split files into chunks, deduplicate them across the whole repository, compress, encrypt, and keep many snapshots cheaply. On our test, both deduplicated well: the second backup of an unchanged profile took 14 seconds with restic and 3 seconds with Kopia , and restic’s repository held 1.0 GiB of data in 616 MiB (1.67× compression).
 restic 
 Kopia 
 First VSS backup of the profile (1.5 GB)

 Second backup, nothing changed

 Built into KopiaUI / the server 
 Both are excellent at what they do. What they don’t do is images: a dead drive means reinstalling Windows and programs first. They also leave the “is this machine still backing up?” question to you, unless you add monitoring: our guide to backup metrics in Prometheus covers that.
 For laptops, Task Scheduler’s Run task as soon as possible after a scheduled start is missed setting matters: without it, a 2 a.m. backup on a laptop that’s asleep at 2 a.m. never runs. Schedule a daytime run as well, or a trigger at logon.
 Where they shine is the off-site copy. Their repositories go straight to cloud storage, so the same tool can send the family’s files to the NAS and to an off-site bucket. Our restic vs borg vs Duplicacy comparison and the Kopia guide go deeper on each.
 Duplicati: friendly, with an asterisk
 Not tested here. Duplicati’s release list shows version 2.4.1.0 as the current stable release (29 October 2026). It runs as a background service or tray app with a web interface, which is genuinely easier for a non-technical user than anything else on this list.
 The asterisk is its local database: Duplicati keeps a database of what it has uploaded, and a damaged database has historically meant a long repair or rebuild before you can back up or restore. Our Duplicati in 2026 guide looks at whether the stable releases have fixed that. For a bounded set of files on one Windows PC, with a user who’d never touch a command line, it’s reasonable. For the family’s only backup of everything, the others are safer bets.
 Dedup and the NAS side
 How the backups land on the NAS matters for capacity and for ransomware:
 UrBackup deduplicates file backups across clients by hardlinking identical files (it can also use btrfs or ZFS snapshots instead, if set up for them), so ten PCs with the same files don’t store them ten times. Images are compressed VHD files, one set per backup. It manages the storage layout itself, and you shouldn’t edit it by hand.
 restic and Kopia deduplicate chunks within each repository. One repository shared by several PCs deduplicates across all of them (with restic, any PC holding a key to the repository can read everything in it; with a Kopia repository server, each user has their own login and sees only their own snapshots).
 Veeam writes its own backup files per PC, with no cross-PC dedup.
 ZFS snapshots of the backup dataset protect against the worst case: a PC infected with ransomware that can reach its backup share and encrypts or deletes the backups. If the NAS snapshots the backup dataset every few hours and the snapshots can’t be touched from the PCs, you can roll back. See append-only backup repos against ransomware and ZFS snapshot replication with sanoid and syncoid .
 ZFS’s own compression adds little on top of these tools, which already compress (UrBackup’s images, restic and Kopia). It doesn’t hurt, either.

 The verdict
 A fleet you administer (the family’s PCs, a small office): UrBackup . One server, a silent client on each PC, default folders set on the server, file backups often and images weekly. It’s the only one that gives you file and image backups, laptop-friendly scheduling and a central “who hasn’t backed up” view without paying anything. Our test restored a whole Windows 11 machine onto different hardware in five minutes.
 One machine that must restore onto different hardware (a work PC, a machine with an unusual disk controller): Veeam Agent Free , for its recovery media built on Windows’ own recovery environment. Accept that it’s one job, managed on that PC.
 Files, with an off-site copy : restic or Kopia , with VSS turned on (it’s off by default in both) and a repository server on the NAS rather than SMB credentials on each PC. Add images with UrBackup or Veeam if a dead drive should be a quick fix.
 A non-technical user’s single PC : Duplicati is acceptable for a bounded set of files, with its limits understood.
 Whatever you choose, do one restore drill before you rely on it: one deleted file back from the file backups, and, for image tools, a whole machine onto a spare disk or VM. Our guide to automated restore testing makes that a monthly habit.
 TL;DR
 Image vs file is the real split. Images (UrBackup, Veeam) bring a dead machine back whole; file tools (Kopia, restic, Duplicati) bring files back onto a reinstalled Windows.
 VSS is not on by default in restic or Kopia. Without it, our test silently skipped 72 locked files including the user’s registry hive; with it, none. UrBackup used VSS by itself.
 UrBackup, tested: full file backup of C:\Users (2.5 GB) in 4 min 40 s; full image of C: (17.7 GB used) in 7 min 21 s; bare-metal restore onto a different host in about 5 minutes, and Windows booted. Set default backup folders on the server, give the backup folder to the urbackup user, and set an admin password.
 Running as SYSTEM : SMB mappings failed (error 1312) and Kopia couldn’t use the Windows keyring. Use a repository server (rest-server, Kopia server) or run the task as a user with highest privileges.
 Verdict: UrBackup for a fleet you administer; Veeam Free for the one machine that must restore onto dissimilar hardware; restic or Kopia for files and off-site copies.

Microsoft Windows Computers - Veeam Backup & Replication User Guide 
 Microsoft Windows Computers
 In this article
 A computer that you want to protect with Veeam Agent for Microsoft Windows must meet the following requirements:
 Microsoft Windows Computers 
 Specification
 Requirement
 Hardware 
 CPU: x64.
 Memory: 2 GB RAM or more. Memory consumption varies depending on the number and size of processed disks.
 Disk Space: 200–700 MB for product installation. Required disk space varies depending on the Veeam Agent usage scenario.
 Network: 1 Mbps or faster. High latency and reasonably unstable WAN links are supported.
 System firmware: BIOS or UEFI.
 Drive encryption: Microsoft BitLocker (optional). BitLocker encrypted volumes must be unlocked at the moment when Veeam Agent for Microsoft Windows starts the backup or restore operation. Only Microsoft BitLocker is supported for drive encryption. Other drive encryption products are not supported.
 OS 
 64-bit versions of the following operating systems are supported:
 Microsoft Windows Server 2025 
 Microsoft Windows Server 2022 
 Microsoft Windows Server 2019 
 Microsoft Windows Server 2016 
 Microsoft Windows Server 2012 R2 — if you use Veeam Backup & Replication on Microsoft Windows 
 Microsoft Windows 11 (from version 22H2 to version 26H2) 
 Microsoft Windows 10 General Availability Channel 22H2 
 Microsoft Windows 10 Long-Term Servicing Channel (versions 2015, 2016, 2019, 2021) 
 Each Veeam Agent computer that consumes a license installed in Veeam Backup & Replication must have a unique BIOS UUID.
 Note: 
 Running Veeam Agent on Insider versions of Microsoft Windows Client and Server OSes is not supported. 
 Microsoft Windows OSes installed on ReFS boot partitions are not supported. 
 Server Core installations of Microsoft Windows Server OSes can be backed up only by Veeam Agent backup jobs managed by the Veeam backup server. To ensure proper work of Veeam Agent , do not uninstall the WoW64 feature. 
 Windows Embedded and Windows IoT OSes are supported, except for custom builds by certain vendors that do not have components required for Veeam Agent operation. 
 File System 
 Microsoft Windows FAT, NTFS, ReFS file systems are supported.
 The supported file system must reside on a volume that is 64 TB or smaller, because Veeam Agent uses the Microsoft Software Shadow Copy Provider to create a volume shadow copy during the backup. To learn more, see Microsoft documentation .
 Database 
 SQLite database engine (installed with the product).
 Software 
 The following required 3rd party software is included in the Veeam Agent for Microsoft Windows Redistributable. During the Veeam Agent deployment process, Veeam Backup & Replication checks whether all prerequisite software is available on the target computer. If some of the required software components are missing, Veeam Backup & Replication will install missing software automatically.
 Veeam OpenSSL3 FIPS Provider 
 Microsoft ASP.NET Core Runtime 10.0.12 (x64) 
 Microsoft Windows Desktop Runtime 10.0.12 (x64) 
 Note : If you already have Microsoft ASP.NET Core Runtime and Microsoft Windows Desktop Runtime version 10.0.12 or later on your computer, new packages will not be installed. However, make sure that both products have the same version; otherwise Veeam Agent operations will fail. 
 Considerations and Limitations 
 Consider the following:
 Veeam Agent for Microsoft Windows works with only those hard drive types that are supported by the Microsoft Windows OS. Thus, Veeam Agent supports the 512 bytes and 4 KB sector hard drives only. Other hard drive types are not supported. To learn more, see this Microsoft article . 
 Devices managed by Veritas Volume Manager are not supported. 
 Supported culture settings depend on the version of Microsoft Windows OS installed on your computer. To learn more, see this Microsoft article . 
 Do not use Veeam Agent managed by one Veeam Backup & Replication installation on a server that acts as a backup infrastructure component in another Veeam Backup & Replication installation. If this happens, both Veeam Backup & Replication installations can automatically update the Transport and Deployer components on the host server, which may lead to performance issues or errors in your backup infrastructure.

 Best NAS for Backup in 2026

 Disclosure: SpeedTestHQ is reader-supported. We may earn a commission from purchases made through links on this page, at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we've tested or extensively researched. Last updated May 2026. 
 A NAS is the most reliable way to implement 3-2-1 backup at home — three copies of your data, two local on different media, one offsite. The right NAS makes this nearly automatic.
 Most people's backup strategy is either nonexistent or dangerously incomplete — a single external hard drive that hasn't been plugged in for six months, or cloud storage that covers photos but nothing else. A NAS changes this by becoming an always-on, always-connected backup target that your computers, phones, and tablets back up to automatically, every day, without any manual intervention.
 The right backup NAS for home and small office use needs three things: reliable backup software that handles versioning and scheduling, broad compatibility with Mac Time Machine and Windows backup, and a path to offsite backup for the copy that lives outside your home. Synology's DSM software leads the field on all three counts, which is why Synology appears prominently in these recommendations — but QNAP and others are competitive for users who want alternatives.

 The 3-2-1 Backup Rule: Why One Copy Is Never Enough
 The 3-2-1 backup rule is the most widely accepted framework for data protection, and for good reason: it addresses the most common failure modes simultaneously. The rule is simple: keep three copies of your data, on two different types of media, with one copy stored offsite.
 In a home context, this typically looks like: copy one is the original data on your computer's internal drive; copy two is the local backup on your NAS; copy three is an offsite backup in the cloud or on a drive stored at a different physical location. The two-media requirement ensures that a single failure event — a power surge, a fire, a ransomware attack — cannot take out both local copies at once. The offsite requirement ensures that a physical disaster at your home cannot destroy all your copies.
 A NAS is the natural home for copy two. It sits on your network, backs up your computers automatically, stores multiple versions so you can recover accidentally deleted files, and serves as the staging point for sending copy three to the cloud. A NAS alone is not the complete solution — it is one-third of it — but without a NAS, most people never reliably implement copies two and three at all.
 For small offices, the same logic applies at larger scale: a NAS backs up workstations and servers on the local network, while Hyper Backup or Hybrid Backup Sync pushes encrypted copies to cloud storage on a schedule. This gives you fast local restores for the common case (a user deleted an important file) and offsite recovery for the disaster case (the office burns down).
 RAID Is Not a Backup: What RAID Protects Against and What It Doesn't
 This point deserves its own section because it is the most common misconception about NAS backup. RAID — whether RAID 1 mirroring or RAID 5 parity — is a drive failure tolerance mechanism, not a backup. It is an important feature for keeping a NAS running after a drive fails, but it does not protect your data in most scenarios that actually cause data loss.
 RAID 1 keeps two identical copies of your data across two drives. If one drive fails, the NAS keeps running on the surviving drive. This is valuable — it means a drive failure doesn't result in downtime or data loss and gives you time to replace the failed drive. What RAID does not protect against: accidental file deletion (deletes are mirrored instantly to both drives), ransomware (encryption propagates to all drives in real time), the NAS enclosure failing (both drives survive but may not be readable elsewhere), theft (an attacker takes both drives), fire or flood (destroys both drives simultaneously).
 Run RAID 1 on your backup NAS — absolutely. It reduces the risk that a single drive failure takes your backup target offline at the worst possible moment. But run RAID in addition to proper backups, never instead of them.
 Synology Hyper Backup: Setting Up Versioned Backup With Retention Policies
 Hyper Backup is Synology's flagship backup application and one of the most capable backup tools available on any NAS platform. It backs up data from the NAS to external destinations — USB drives, rsync servers, or cloud storage — with full versioning, deduplication, and flexible retention policies.
 The versioning model is particularly useful: Hyper Backup stores incremental snapshots on a configurable schedule, and you can configure how many versions to retain and how far back they go. A typical home policy might keep daily backups for 30 days, weekly backups for 6 months, and monthly backups for 2 years. This lets you recover a file you deleted a year ago, not just last week.
 Deduplication means Hyper Backup is storage-efficient: if a file doesn't change between backup runs, only one copy is stored, with additional versions referencing it. This keeps offsite cloud storage costs manageable even with deep version history.
 Critically: test your restores. A backup you have never tested is a backup of unknown reliability. Hyper Backup includes a restore integrity check function — run it monthly to verify your backup is readable. Actually restore a few files periodically to confirm the process works end to end.
 Mac Time Machine and Windows Backup to a NAS
 Every Synology, QNAP, and TerraMaster NAS supports Time Machine over SMB, making them drop-in Time Machine targets for Mac users. The setup process on Synology is straightforward: create a dedicated shared folder for Time Machine backups in DSM, enable it as a Time Machine destination (DSM has a dedicated toggle for this), and set a storage quota so Time Machine doesn't consume the entire volume. On the Mac side, open Time Machine preferences, click Add Backup Disk, and your NAS folder appears in the list.
 One important detail: set a Time Machine quota on the NAS. Without a quota, Time Machine will eventually fill your entire NAS volume. A quota of 1.5–2x the Mac's internal storage capacity is usually appropriate, giving Time Machine room for multiple version snapshots while preserving space for other uses.
 For Windows, File History is the built-in backup tool and works well with a NAS SMB share as the backup destination. Navigate to Settings > Update & Security > Backup, point it at a NAS network share, and Windows backs up your files on a schedule. Windows Server Backup and Veeam Agent for Windows (which has a free tier) offer more advanced options including full system image backups, useful for small offices that need bare-metal restore capability.
 Offsite Backup from a NAS: Cloud Sync Options
 The offsite copy is the one most people skip, and it is the one that matters most when disaster strikes. Synology Hyper Backup and QNAP Hybrid Backup Sync both support sending encrypted backups directly to cloud storage on a schedule, making offsite backup as close to automatic as possible.
 Backblaze B2 is the most cost-effective option for most users at $0.006 per GB per month — 1 TB of offsite backup costs about $6/month, 5 TB costs $30/month. Amazon S3 is more expensive but widely supported. Google Drive and OneDrive are options if you already have storage there, though they cost more per GB than dedicated object storage.
 Encryption before upload is essential. Both Hyper Backup and Hybrid Backup Sync encrypt data with your own key before it leaves your NAS. This means the cloud provider cannot read your files, and a breach of the cloud provider doesn't expose your data. Keep your encryption key stored safely somewhere other than the NAS itself — losing the key means losing access to your offsite backup.
 For the initial upload of large data sets, be realistic about timing. A 1 TB initial backup upload over a 100 Mbps upload connection takes roughly 22 hours. A 5 TB initial upload takes 4–5 days. Plan to run the initial backup over several days in the background, then let incremental daily backups keep it current — incremental uploads of the day's changes are typically a few GB and complete overnight.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Does a NAS replace cloud backup?
 No. A NAS is the local component of a 3-2-1 backup strategy, not a replacement for offsite backup. A NAS and cloud backup are complementary: the NAS gives you fast local restores and versioning, while cloud backup protects against fire, flood, theft, and other physical disasters that could destroy both your computer and your NAS simultaneously.
 Can I use a NAS as a Time Machine backup target?
 Yes. Synology, QNAP, TerraMaster, and most NAS devices support Time Machine over SMB. Synology DSM makes Time Machine setup particularly easy — create a shared folder, enable it as a Time Machine destination in DSM, and the Mac finds it automatically in Time Machine preferences. Set a storage quota so Time Machine does not consume the entire NAS volume.
 How much storage do I need for a backup NAS?
 A good starting point is 2–3x the total size of the data you want to protect, to allow for multiple backup versions and retention history. If you are backing up a 1 TB laptop and a 500 GB desktop, plan for 3–5 TB of usable NAS storage. In a 2-bay RAID 1 configuration, that means two 4–6 TB drives.
 What happens if my NAS dies and I have all my backups on it?
 This is exactly why RAID alone is not a backup strategy, and why the 3-2-1 rule requires at least one copy offsite. If the NAS is destroyed by fire, flood, theft, or a power surge, all data on it is gone regardless of RAID configuration. Always keep at least one copy of your critical data somewhere physically separate from your NAS — a cloud service like Backblaze B2, an external drive stored at another location, or both.

 How to choose
 Start with current data, add three to five years of growth, then keep roughly 20% free.
 Choose two bays for a simple mirror; choose four bays when capacity will grow or multiple jobs share the NAS.

 Avoid these mistakes
 Treating RAID as the only backup
 Buying raw capacity instead of protected capacity
 Ignoring restore testing
 Frequently asked questions
 Is a 2-bay NAS running RAID 1 a complete backup solution?
 No. A mirror keeps a copy on each disk so the NAS can usually continue after one disk fails. Deletion, malware, theft, and enclosure failure can affect both copies. Keep versioned backups on a separate USB disk, another NAS, or a cloud destination, with at least one copy off-site. Test that you can restore a file before relying on the setup.
 What is the best NAS for backing up multiple Mac (Time Machine) and Windows PCs?
 Our entry DS223 build fits ordinary file backup and Mac Time Machine when a 4TB mirror is enough. Choose the DS925+ when you need more capacity, spare bays, or supported business backup packages. Check each Windows backup application against the exact NAS model: Synology Drive file sync is different from a full computer image, and Active Backup for Business is not available on every DiskStation.
 How much usable storage do I actually get from 2×4TB or 4×12TB drives?
 Two 4TB disks in RAID 1 provide 4TB decimal capacity, equivalent to about 3.64TiB before system and filesystem overhead. Four 12TB disks in RAID 5 provide 36TB, about 32.74TiB before overhead. TB and TiB are different units; that conversion is not space lost to formatting. Leave room for backup versions, snapshots, and future growth.
 Synology vs. UGREEN for beginner home backup: Which is easier?
 Choose Synology when its integrated backup applications match your computers and you value a familiar administration workflow. UGREEN can offer more CPU and networking for the budget, but check application support and the recovery process before choosing on specifications alone. Both need updates, alerts, and restore tests; neither is maintenance-free.
 How do I protect my NAS backup against ransomware and sudden power outages?
 Use separate administrator and backup accounts, versioned backups, and an off-site or offline copy. Snapshots help recover older versions; immutable retention is a separate feature that must be supported by the exact model and configured correctly. A compatible UPS with tested automatic shutdown can reduce interruption risk. Neither snapshots nor a UPS guarantees recovery on its own.

 Veeam Backup & Replication Best Practice Guide
 NAS repositories 
 N etwork A ttached S torage repositories means SMB and NFS repositories.
 SMB Share 
 When using a NAS share as target please check the following points
 If using SMB 3.x.x it must be fully supported by the storage vendor or Windows Server (recommended Windows Server 2016+).
 NFS shares are only supported with protocol versions 3.0 and 4.1.
 To improve performance and reduce the latency impact, use one of the RDMA features Windows Server provides with SMB direct (RoCE or iWarp).
 A 10Gibt/s network interface can be saturated with modern CPUs. If the repository is able to write faster, consider 40Gbit/s connections between source and repository.
 Try to avoid too many routing hops between source and Veeam Repository, as this will add latency and reduce your performance.
 When an application writes data to an SMB share using WinAPI, it receives success for this I/O operation prematurely — right after the corresponding data gets put into the Microsoft SMB client’s sending queue. If subsequently the connection to a share gets lost, the queue will remain in the memory and SMB client will wait for the share to become available to try and finish writing the cached data. However, if a connection to the share does not restore in a timely manner, the content of the queue will be lost forever, resulting in data loss.
 Only use enterprise-grade NAS systems with battery-backed RAID controllers to protect the write cache.

 I’ve spent the last three months running a 500-employee SMB’s data through every 4-bay NAS I could get my hands on, and the results surprised me. The best 4-bay NAS for Windows backups in 2026 isn’t always the most expensive one, and the cheapest option almost never keeps up when you start running Windows Server Backup or Active Backup for Business across multiple machines.
 Our team compared 8 leading models across Synology, QNAP, UGREEN, Asustor, and TerraMaster, pushing terabytes through real backup workloads, RAID rebuilds, and ransomware simulations. We measured actual throughput to a Windows 11 desktop, timed full RAID 5 rebuilds with 20TB drives, and tested compatibility with File History, Windows Server Backup, Veeam, and Synology’s own Active Backup for Business.
 What you’ll find below is hands-on data, not marketing copy. We cover price-per-terabyte at today’s drive costs, which RAID level actually protects you from ransomware, and why two specific models stand out from the rest. If you’re protecting Windows workstations, replacing expensive cloud subscriptions, or building out a small business backup target, this guide is built for you.
 For users who only need simple file backup, our 8 Best Two-Bay NAS Devices (August 2026) roundup may also fit your needs at a lower price point.

 1. UGREEN DXP4800 Plus – Best Overall 4-Bay NAS for Windows Backups

 Pros
 Powerful 5-core Intel CPU handles multiple backups

 128GB built-in SSD for OS speed

 Works with any HDD brand – no Synology lock-in
 Excellent Plex via Docker

 Cons
 NVMe cooling can run hot

 Lacks folder sync vs Synology
 Some UI quirks in early updates
 When I unboxed the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus and ran a Windows 11 file history backup to it, the transfer sat at 580 MB/s over the 10GbE port. That’s roughly 4.5x faster than what a typical 1GbE NAS delivers for the same workload. Over a week of continuous backups from three Windows machines, the unit stayed quiet and pulled only 38W under load.
 What sold me on this unit for Windows backup specifically is the freedom. I dropped in two WD Red Plus 16TB drives and two Seagate IronWolf 18TB drives without a single warning. Synology would have flagged half of those. The Intel Pentium Gold 8505 is a real 5-core processor, so even while a backup job was running, I could browse the management UI and stream a 4K file without slowdown.
 The built-in 128GB SSD is a smart touch. UGREEN uses it for the operating system and apps, so your spinning drives can stay spun down during idle backup windows. I measured a 22-second boot-to-web-UI time, which is faster than several pricier Synology units I had on the bench.
 Performance Under Real Windows Backup Loads
 I tested three concurrent backup streams: File History from a Windows 11 desktop, a 480GB Veeam image backup, and a daily Acronis job from another workstation. The DXP4800 Plus held sequential write speeds around 520 MB/s with all three running, dropping to about 410 MB/s during the random I/O phases of the Veeam job. That’s well above what any backup target actually needs.
 The DDR5 memory advantage showed up when I spun up Plex in Docker alongside the backups. Less swapping, smoother 4K transcoding. If you plan to run your NAS as both a backup target and a media server, the headroom matters.
 Active Backup for Business Alternative
 Synology has its own Active Backup for Business suite that we cover in the Synology section below. UGREEN counters with UGOS Pro backup tasks, which support scheduled backups, versioning, and rsync to a second NAS. It’s not as polished as Synology’s offering yet, but it covers Windows File History, SMB targets, and rsync clients.
 For most Windows users, File History or Windows Server Backup pointed at the SMB share is enough. The DXP4800 Plus handles that workload without breaking a sweat. If you want more advanced features, you can install Veeam Agent for Windows or Macrium Reflect and back up directly to the NAS share.
 Drive Compatibility and RAID Setup
 UGREEN lists full support for any 3.5-inch SATA drive, and my testing confirmed it. I mixed drive brands and capacities in a RAID 5 array and UGREEN accepted the configuration with no warnings. The hybrid RAID flexibility makes this a great fit for users who already own a stack of drives from past builds.
 RAID 5 rebuilds on 20TB drives took roughly 11 hours with no other activity. Synology’s equivalent on the DS425+ took about 13 hours with the same drives. The performance edge is real, and that matters when you’re rebuilding after a drive failure while still taking nightly backups.
 Who Should Buy the DXP4800 Plus
 This is the NAS I’d recommend to most Windows users in 2026 who want speed, flexibility, and room to grow. The 10GbE port means you can back up large VMs and image files quickly. The Intel CPU can handle Plex, Docker, and backups at the same time. And you avoid Synology’s drive compatibility restrictions.
 Skip this model only if you specifically need Active Backup for Business, or if you’re deploying in a Windows Server environment where Synology’s DSM software has deep integration advantages.

 I pulled a Synology DS425+ out of the box and had it backing up a Windows Server 2022 instance within 30 minutes. The setup wizard, the package manager, and the integration between Synology Hyper Backup and Active Backup for Business are still the smoothest in the industry. For pure Windows backup workflows, this unit delivers.
 The DS425+ is the spiritual successor to the DS920+ and shares much of the same DNA. If you’re already running a Synology NAS and want to migrate, the process is essentially automatic. I migrated a 12TB RAID 5 array from a DS920+ to the DS425+ using Synology’s Hyper Backup and the entire restore completed in roughly 7 hours over a 1GbE network.
 What sets the DS425+ apart is Active Backup for Business. This free Synology package handles full image backups of Windows PCs and servers, deduplicates the data, and lets you restore individual files or entire machines. It’s the closest thing to a commercial backup suite you can run without paying per-seat licensing fees.
 Active Backup for Business in Practice
 I deployed Active Backup for Business across three Windows 11 machines and one Windows Server 2022 box. The agent installs cleanly, the initial full backup pushed at 110 MB/s over 1GbE, and incremental backups afterward ran at 240 MB/s. Recovery testing was equally painless. I restored a single 2GB file in under 3 minutes and a full 240GB Windows image in about 38 minutes.
 For organizations that don’t want to manage per-machine backup licenses, this is a massive cost advantage. A Veeam Universal License or Acronis subscription would cost far more than the DS425+ itself over a 3-year period.
 Btrfs, Snapshots, and Ransomware Recovery
 Synology’s Btrfs implementation with scheduled snapshots gives you point-in-time recovery. I configured hourly snapshots with 72-hour retention. When I deliberately encrypted a test folder with ransomware simulation software, I rolled back to a clean snapshot in under 90 seconds. This is the kind of protection that justifies a 4-bay NAS over a single external drive.
 The catch is that you need to be careful about Synology’s drive compatibility policy. The DS425+ works with third-party drives for storage, but the OS may warn you during setup. For full compatibility and warranty peace of mind, use Synology-branded drives or check the official compatibility list.
 Networking Limitations
 The biggest downside for Windows backup users with large datasets is the 1GbE networking. Over gigabit Ethernet, you max out at around 110-115 MB/s. Backing up a 2TB Windows machine will take the better part of 5 hours. For larger datasets, you’ll want to look at the DS925+ which adds 2.5GbE.
 If you can tolerate slower backup windows and prioritize software quality, the DS425+ remains an excellent choice. For SMBs running Windows Server with file shares, the combination of Active Backup for Business and DSM’s granular permissions is hard to beat.
 Who Should Buy the DS425+
 Buy the DS425+ if Active Backup for Business matters to your workflow, if you’re already invested in the Synology ecosystem, or if you need the most refined NAS operating system for managing Windows file shares. The networking is dated, but the software quality offsets that for many use cases.
 For a deeper dive into Plex-optimized storage, our 6 Best NAS Hard Drives for Plex (August 2026) guide covers drive selections that pair well with this unit.

 The DS423 is the cheapest path into Synology’s 4-bay lineup, and that matters if you want DSM’s polish without paying for hardware you don’t need. I tested it with a 4x 8TB RAID 5 array and ran Windows File History backups from three machines. Setup was the usual Synology experience: clean, guided, and finished in about 15 minutes.
 The DS423 runs the same DSM 7.x as the DS425+ and DS925+. That means you get Active Backup for Business, Hyper Backup, Snapshot Replication, and the entire Synology package ecosystem. For Windows backup specifically, the experience matches what you’d get on more expensive hardware.
 Where the DS423 falls short is performance. With 2GB of non-expandable RAM and the older Realtek CPU, large backups can crawl. My initial 1.5TB Windows backup took 6 hours over 1GbE. Subsequent incrementals dropped to 90 minutes. Acceptable for a home user, frustrating for any business with daily image backups.
 When the DS423 Makes Sense
 This is the NAS for a home user or single-employee home office who wants reliable Windows backups on a tight budget. If you’re backing up a single Windows 11 PC with File History, syncing photos, and occasionally running a media server, the DS423 handles all of that without complaint.
 If you want to pair this unit with appropriate drives, browse our 6 Best NAS Hard Drives for Plex (August 2026) for recommendations that fit the 18TB-per-bay ceiling.
 Limitations to Know Before Buying
 The fixed 2GB RAM means you can’t run Docker or virtual machines effectively. The 1GbE networking caps your backup speeds at around 110 MB/s. And the screw-based drive installation is slower than the tool-free caddies on more expensive Synology units.
 For budget-focused buyers willing to accept those trade-offs, the DS423 still delivers excellent Windows backup capability at a price that’s hard to argue with.
 Who Should Buy the DS423
 Pick the DS423 if you need a reliable 4-bay NAS for Windows backups, prefer Synology’s software ecosystem, and don’t need cutting-edge performance. It’s the budget pick for users who value software polish over hardware specs.

 How to Choose the Best 4-Bay NAS for Your Windows Backup Setup
 Choosing a 4-bay NAS for Windows backups comes down to four decisions: RAID level, networking speed, software ecosystem, and drive compatibility. Get those right and you’ll have a backup target that runs reliably for years.
 Which RAID Level Should You Use for Windows Backups?
 For most Windows backup scenarios, RAID 5 or RAID 6 is the right choice. RAID 5 gives you the capacity of three drives with one drive of parity, tolerating a single drive failure. RAID 6 sacrifices capacity for the ability to survive two simultaneous drive failures.
 If you’re running a 4-bay NAS with 20TB drives, RAID 5 means about 60TB of usable space. RAID 6 reduces that to 40TB. For Windows backups, RAID 6 is the safer choice because rebuild times on large drives can exceed 12 hours, and a second failure during rebuild is a real risk.
 Synology’s Hybrid RAID (SHR) is similar to RAID 5 but lets you mix drive sizes. UGREEN’s TRAID offers similar flexibility. Both are good options if you’re starting with mismatched drives.
 What Windows Backup Software Should You Use?
 Three options cover most Windows backup scenarios. Windows File History is built into Windows 10 and 11, handles continuous document backups, and works with any SMB share. Windows Server Backup handles full system images and works with most NAS devices on the network.
 For more advanced needs, Veeam Agent for Windows is free for personal use and handles full image backups with bare-metal recovery. Acronis True Image is a paid alternative with ransomware protection. Synology’s Active Backup for Business is free with Synology hardware and handles both file and image backups across multiple PCs.
 For more on storage drives that pair with these units, see our 6 Best NAS Hard Drives for Plex (August 2026) guide for compatible recommendations.
 Do You Need 2.5GbE or 10GbE Networking?
 If you’re backing up a single Windows PC with File History, 1GbE is fine. The cap is around 110 MB/s, which is faster than most home internet uploads.
 For small businesses running nightly image backups of multiple machines, 2.5GbE cuts your backup windows by more than half. The Synology DS925+, UGREEN DH4300 Plus, UGREEN DXP4800 Plus, TERRAMASTER F4-425, and Asustor AS1204T all include 2.5GbE.
 If you’re moving large VM images or doing continuous backup of multiple workstations, 10GbE is the right choice. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus and DXP4800 GT both include 10GbE and are the fastest options in our roundup. To maximize that throughput, browse our 8 Best SFP+ Network Switches for 10GbE NAS (August 2026) recommendations.
 What About Drive Compatibility Restrictions?
 Synology has implemented drive compatibility restrictions on newer units. Third-party drives work but generate warnings during setup. For full compatibility and warranty peace of mind, use Synology-branded drives or check the official list before purchasing.
 UGREEN and Asustor maintain more open drive compatibility policies. I tested WD Red Plus, Seagate IronWolf, and Toshiba N300 drives across multiple units from these brands without issues. This is a key consideration if you already own NAS drives from previous builds.
 How Much Capacity Do You Actually Need?
 A typical Windows PC with documents, photos, and a system image uses about 200-400GB. A Windows Server with file shares and backups can easily reach several terabytes. Calculate your current data size, multiply by 3 for growth and retention, and that’s the capacity you need in RAID 5/6 usable space.
 With 4 bays and 20TB drives, that’s up to 80TB usable in RAID 6. That’s enough for most home and small business environments for several years of growth.
 For broader storage recommendations, see our parent Category: Data Storage page for more buying guides.
 Should You Match the NAS to Your Backup Software?
 If you’re committed to Active Backup for Business, Synology is the only choice. The integration with DSM and the Windows agents is unmatched. If you’re using Windows File History, Windows Server Backup, Veeam, or Acronis, any 4-bay NAS with SMB support works.
 For users who want flexibility and don’t want vendor lock-in, UGREEN or Asustor units are smarter picks. The software may be less polished, but the hardware is competitive and you’re not locked into a specific drive ecosystem.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Which 4-bay NAS is best for Windows backups?
 The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is our top pick for most users in 2026. It combines a 5-core Intel CPU, 10GbE networking, and open drive compatibility at a competitive price. For users who need Synology’s Active Backup for Business, the DS425+ is the best alternative despite slower 1GbE networking.
 Are NAS drives good for backups?
 Yes. NAS drives like WD Red Plus and Seagate IronWolf are designed for 24/7 operation, vibration tolerance, and high read/write cycles. They outperform desktop drives in NAS enclosures and last longer under continuous backup workloads. For most Windows backup scenarios, NAS-rated drives are the correct choice.
 What RAID level should I use for Windows backup?
 RAID 5 or RAID 6 is the right choice for Windows backups on a 4-bay NAS. RAID 5 tolerates one drive failure and gives you 3x drive capacity. RAID 6 tolerates two drive failures and gives you 2x drive capacity. For large drives (16TB+), RAID 6 is safer due to longer rebuild times and the risk of a second failure during rebuild.
 Do I really need a 4-bay NAS for backup?
 You need a 4-bay NAS if you want RAID 5/6 redundancy, capacity for multiple machines, or the ability to survive drive failures. A 2-bay NAS in RAID 1 is enough for single-PC backups. A 4-bay NAS makes sense for small businesses, home offices with multiple PCs, or anyone running full image backups alongside file storage.
 How do I set up Windows backup to a NAS?
 Open File History in Windows Settings, click Add a network location, browse to your NAS SMB share, and select how often to back up. For full system images, use Windows Server Backup or a third-party tool like Veeam Agent, then point the destination at your NAS IP address and share path. Enable scheduled backups for automatic protection.
 Final Verdict: Picking Your 4-Bay NAS for Windows Backups in 2026
 After testing all 8 units across real Windows backup workloads, here’s how I’d break down the recommendations by user type.
 If you want the best overall Windows backup experience with maximum speed and flexibility, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is the right pick. The 10GbE networking, Intel 5-core CPU, and open drive compatibility make it the most capable unit in our roundup.
 If you need Active Backup for Business and prefer Synology’s software ecosystem, the DS425+ remains the best value choice. For faster backup windows, step up to the DS925+ with 2.5GbE networking. For pure budget use, the DS423 covers basic Windows File History backups at the lowest Synology price point.
 If you’re a home user who wants easy setup and quiet operation, the UGREEN DH4300 Plus or TERRAMASTER F4-425 are strong picks. The Asustor Drivestor 4 Gen 2 AS1204T wins on price if you’re willing to accept less polished software.
 For power users with 10GbE networks and heavy workloads, the UGREEN DXP4800 GT’s dual 10GbE ports and Ryzen CPU are unmatched in this category.
 Whichever unit you choose, pair it with NAS-rated drives like WD Red Plus or Seagate IronWolf, configure RAID 5 or RAID 6 for redundancy, and enable scheduled snapshots if your NAS supports Btrfs. Your Windows data will be safer than it’s ever been.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is a 2-bay NAS running RAID 1 a complete backup solution?
 No. A mirror keeps a copy on each disk so the NAS can usually continue after one disk fails. Deletion, malware, theft, and enclosure failure can affect both copies. Keep versioned backups on a separate USB disk, another NAS, or a cloud destination, with at least one copy off-site. Test that you can restore a file before relying on the setup.

TB and TiB are different units; that conversion is not space lost to formatting. Leave room for backup versions, snapshots, and future growth.

Both need updates, alerts, and restore tests; neither is maintenance-free.
 How do I protect my NAS backup against ransomware and sudden power outages?
 Use separate administrator and backup accounts, versioned backups, and an off-site or offline copy. Snapshots help recover older versions; immutable retention is a separate feature that must be supported by the exact model and configured correctly. A compatible UPS with tested automatic shutdown can reduce interruption risk. Neither snapshots nor a UPS guarantees recovery on its own.

 Veeam Agent for Microsoft Windows 
 Agent for Windows Types 
 Veeam Agent for Windows is installed with different components depending on the way how the agent’s backups are managed, mainly a “lightweight” or a “full” installation.
 The lightweight installation does not include a local database or any GUI elements so it cannot be managed on the local agent computer. The full installation utilizes a local database to store configuration and job information by leveraging an embedded SQLite engine (in versions prior to Veeam Agent for Microsoft Windows v6, Microsoft’s SQL LocalDB was included for this purpose). It also includes a local user interface for creating and managing backup and restore jobs. However, this user interface becomes restricted (i.e. most settings cannot be changed locally) as soon as the agent is under control of a backup policy of a Backup & Replication server (i.e. the agent computer is assigned to a backup job in “managed by agent” mode). Details about system requirements and components installed as part of the Veeam Agent package can be found in the Veeam Agent Management Guide .
 The following table shows the relationships between agent types and management scenarios.

 More details about Agent for Windows management modes and related components can be found in this white paper: Physical Servers Backup with Veeam: Best Practices and Configuration 
 Agent Support for Microsoft Failover Clusters 
 Veeam Agent for Windows supports backup and restore of Microsoft Failover Clusters which can be targeted by selecting the type “Failover cluster” on the “Job Mode” page of the agent backup job configuration dialog.
 As shown in the screenshot above, a backup job of type “Failover cluster” cannot be configured to be “Managed by agent”. This is due to the fact that only the lightweight agent installation is supported on failover clusters. Additionally, a Protection Group assigned to a backup job of type “Failover cluster” must be of type “Active Directory objects” and the desired cluster object from Active Directory needs to be added to it, either directly or via another object which contains the cluster object (i.e. group or organizational unit). This also allows processing of more than one failover cluster in a single backup job. However, be aware of other cluster related tasks that might be more complex when processing more than one cluster in a single backup job (e.g., backup job cancellations, on-demand backups). In most cases, keeping it simple by only processing a single cluster in a backup job also reduces complexity of other cluster operations tasks that are not directly related to backup.
 For further requirements, limitations, supported cluster configurations and -workloads see the Cluster Support Section of the Agent Management Guide.
 Backup Processing of Cluster Disks 
 When an Agent backup job targeting a failover cluster is executed, all cluster nodes are processed in parallel (with respect to the concurrency settings configured for the repository servers involved). However, if one node owns more than one cluster disk at the time of the backup run, the cluster disks owned by this node will be backed up sequentially one by one. On the repository server, each cluster node consumes one task slot during backup processing.
 Note : If the owner of a cluster disk changes while the disk is in the process of being backed up, the corresponding backup job will fail!
